# DIT Dara Initiative Tech (DIT)

> Dara Initiative Technology builds open models, offline-first AI and EdTech for communities where connectivity and power are uncertain. Based in Oyo State, Nigeria. All technical claims in our writing trace to primary sources (P1), independent benchmarks (P2) or clearly-labelled community leads (P3).

## Key pages

- [Home](https://dintechnologies.com/): Dara Initiative Technology: open models, offline AI and EdTech for Africa
- [Blog](https://dintechnologies.com/blog): Notes on open models, local infrastructure and practical AI
- [OpenModel Synthesis Framework (OMSF)](https://dintechnologies.com/framework): The six-rung Openness Ladder for grading open AI models
- [Open Model Leaderboard](https://dintechnologies.com/open-models): Leading open models graded on the OMSF ladder
- [Reports Library](https://dintechnologies.com/reports): Ready-made OMSF-audited model reports
- [Research](https://dintechnologies.com/research): Academic and industry sources behind OMSF
- [EduTech / SomaBox](https://dintechnologies.com/edutech): Offline AI tutor for schools, zero internet required
- [AI Training Hub](https://dintechnologies.com/ai-hub): Hands-on AI training in Nigeria
- [S-SME](https://dintechnologies.com/s-sme): Sustainable SME services: green energy, offline inventory, compliance
- [S-SME Toolkit](https://dintechnologies.com/s-sme/toolkit): 117-item scored toolkit with fillable PDFs
- [S-SME Evidence](https://dintechnologies.com/s-sme/evidence): Published sources behind the S-SME numbers
- [About](https://dintechnologies.com/about): Mission, ecosystem and team of Dara Initiative Technology
- [Contact](https://dintechnologies.com/contact): Reach DIT

## Blog posts

- [Community-built giants: BLOOM and the RAIL license](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/history-open-local-private-ai-bloom-rail): How the BigScience workshop proved massive open models could be built by communities, while introducing the complications of use-based licensing.
- [Stable Diffusion: open weights build AI ecosystems](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/history-open-local-private-ai-stable-diffusion): How the August 2022 release of Stable Diffusion proved that open model weights trigger rapid ecosystem innovation that closed APIs cannot match.
- [GPT-2 and the first staged AI release](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/history-open-local-private-ai-gpt2-staged-release): How OpenAI’s 2019 decision to withhold GPT-2 turned model release from an engineering afterthought into a primary policy debate.
- [Offline-first parent-teacher portals, explained](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/offline-first-parent-teacher-portals): Most parent-teacher portals go dark the moment the connection drops. For families who rely on them most, offline-first design is the difference between a tool that works and one that does not.
- [What "open-source AI" means after 2025](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/what-open-source-ai-means-after-2025-license-shifts): In 2025 several models were called open while their licenses said otherwise. For any organisation that wants to self-host, that gap decides who sees your data, what you pay, and whether the system keeps running.
- [The LLaMA leak and an accidental case study in risk](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/history-open-local-private-ai-llama-leak): How the March 2023 leak of Meta’s LLaMA model provided a documented case study of what happens when AI is released without proper risk review.
- [Mistral and the deliberate-open counter-move](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/history-open-local-private-ai-mistral-open-sovereignty): How Mistral AI used a permissive Apache 2.0 release to make a strategic argument for European AI sovereignty, setting a precedent for global public sector procurement.
- [DeepSeek R1 and the compute-efficiency shock](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/history-open-local-private-ai-deepseek-r1): How a January 2025 model release trained under chip export restrictions proved that frontier AI development does not require Silicon Valley capital.
- [The measurement problem: from gradient to framework](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/history-open-local-private-ai-measurement-framework): How the chaos of staged releases and accidental leaks forced academics to build real measurement systems for open artificial intelligence.
- [Regulation catches up: defining open source AI](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/history-open-local-private-ai-regulation-catches-up): How the 2024 EU AI Act and the Open Source AI Definition forced legal teams to treat open model licenses as serious compliance risks.
- [The Global South chapter and the reality of local AI](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/history-open-local-private-ai-global-south): How a World Bank-backed pilot in Nigeria proves that local AI deployment solves fundamental infrastructure gaps where cloud APIs fail.
- [The closing door: does openness survive 2026?](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/history-open-local-private-ai-closing-door): As signals suggest the lab that catalyzed the open weight movement might pull back, the industry faces a live question about the future of open AI.
- [What open models actually cost to run](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/mid-year-cost-reality-check): Running an open model on your own hardware trades a fixed cost for a variable one. Whether that saves money depends on your volume, and the honest answer is contested. Here is the mid-year check, with the hardware and license claims checked against named sources.
- [What open-source models are (and when to use them)](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/what-are-open-source-models): Most AI you use today is rented, not owned. Open-source models change that. Here is what they are, who should care, and why the conversation matters now.
- [Why we build offline-first, not cloud-first](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/why-we-build-offline-first): The cloud is treated as a given. For much of the world it is not. Here is the engineering and moral case for designing without it.
- [The quiet cost of vendor lock-in](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/the-quiet-cost-of-vendor-lock-in): Lock-in is rarely a dramatic event. It is a slow tax on every decision. A short field note on why ownership beats rental.
- [The Openness Ladder: 4 levels of open-source AI](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/the-openness-ladder): The label "open source" now covers at least four different things. If you cannot place a model on a ladder, you cannot make a safe decision about it. We built one.
- [Running open models privately: a deployment guide](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/running-open-models-privately): You can run a capable model on hardware you own, with no API and no data leaving the building. Here is the technical path, with the 2025 tooling.
- [Open models for the public sector and non-profits](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/open-models-public-sector): For governments and non-profits, openness is not ideology. It is procurement law, data sovereignty and the ability to serve people the cloud forgot.
- [NVIDIA Nemotron 3: CUDA-first open AI](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/nemotron-3-profile): Nemotron 3 Ultra and Super are NVIDIA's open-weight CUDA-first models: around 550B and smaller, with long context and heavy NVIDIA optimizations. This post covers what they are and what they take to run.
- [Qwen3.5 397B: Apache open generalist](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/qwen-3-5-397b-profile): Qwen3.5-397B-A17B is Alibaba's Apache 2.0 mid-to-large open generalist: 397B total, 17B active, 256K context, and strong multilingual coverage. This post covers what it is and what it takes to run.
- [Inkling: Thinking Machines' open 1M model](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/thinking-machines-inkling-profile): Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab is the ~975B open-weight entrant with a 1M context: competitive mid-to-high ranks, built for long-context research and agents. Here is what it is and what it takes to run.
- [Xiaomi MiMo V2.5: the coding value MoE](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/mimo-v2-5-profile): MiMo V2.5 is Xiaomi's open-weight 1T-scale MoE with a 1M context and a strong coding-story, released under permissive terms. Here is the practical read on what it is and whether it belongs in your stack.
- [Kimi K2.6: the open coding specialist](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/kimi-k2-6-profile): Kimi K2.6 is Moonshot's previous-generation 1T open model and the proven coding and agentic specialist that still ships in production. This is the practical guide to what it is and when to choose it.
- [Phi-4: laptop-sized open AI](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/phi-4-profile): Phi-4 is Microsoft's ~14B open model built for edge and laptop AI: strong reasoning per size, MIT-style licensing, and the lowest hardware bar in this series. This is the full practical guide.
- [gpt-oss-120b: OpenAI's Apache model](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/gpt-oss-120b-profile): gpt-oss-120b is OpenAI's fully open Apache 2.0 release: 117B total, 5.1B active, with a lower intelligence rank than 2026's Chinese flagships but a clean legal story. Here is the practical read.
- [Llama 4 Maverick: Meta's open flagship](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/llama-4-maverick-profile): Llama 4 Maverick pairs a 400B open-weight MoE with a 1M context and native multimodality, inside Meta's deep tooling ecosystem. Here is what it is, what its license allows, and what it takes to run it.
- [Mistral Small 4 & Medium 3.5: EU AI](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/mistral-small-4-medium-3-5-profile): Mistral Small 4 and Medium 3.5 are the efficient, Apache-leaning open models from Europe. This post covers what they are, why they fit EU data-residency requirements, and what they take to run.
- [Llama 4 Scout: open model, 10M context](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/llama-4-scout-profile): Llama 4 Scout has the largest open context window at 10M tokens. Here is what the model is, what makes its context special, what the community license allows, and what it takes to run it.
- [Qwen3.6 27B: local coding assistant](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/qwen-3-6-profile): Qwen3.6 (27B dense and 35B-A3B MoE) is the Apache 2.0 sweet spot for private coding assistants on modest hardware. This is what it is, what it needs, and what it takes to run.
- [Gemma 4 31B: one-GPU open multimodal](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/gemma-4-31b-profile): Gemma 4 31B is Google DeepMind's Apache 2.0 model that fits on one high-end GPU: strong code and reasoning, native multimodal, and the cleanest license in its size class. This is the full practical guide.
- [GLM-5.1: MIT open model, still in service](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/glm-5-1-profile): GLM-5.1 is the MIT-licensed predecessor to GLM-5.2: roughly 744B total, 40B active, 200K context, and still a sane production choice when you want a clean license at mid-tier scale. Here is the breakdown.
- [MiniMax M3: 1M-context open AI](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/minimax-m3-profile): MiniMax M3 is a 428B open-weight MoE with a 1M context and multimodal capability, competitive on generalist leaderboards. This is the practical guide to what it is and whether it fits your stack.
- [Tencent Hy3: open model worth evaluating](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/tencent-hy3-profile): Tencent Hy3 is the mid-tier open-weight model that keeps appearing on 2026 leaderboards. Here is what it is, what it needs, and what to check in its license before you adopt it.
- [DeepSeek V4 Flash: open AI workhorse](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/deepseek-v4-flash-profile): DeepSeek V4 Flash is the MIT-licensed high-volume workhorse of 2026: 284B total, 13B active, 1M context, and one of the best tokens-per-dollar profiles when self-hosted. Here is the full practical breakdown.
- [GLM-5.2: MIT open model for agentic coding](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/glm-5-2-profile): GLM-5.2 from Z.ai gives you a near-frontier open model with a clean MIT license: roughly 750B total, 40B active, 1M context, built for long agentic coding. Here is what it takes to run it.
- [DeepSeek V4 Pro: open MIT frontier AI](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/deepseek-v4-pro-profile): DeepSeek V4 Pro is the strongest MIT-licensed open model in 2026: 1.6T total parameters, 49B active, 1M context, no revenue gates. Here is what it is, what it runs on, and what it takes to self-host.
- [Kimi K3: open 1M-context multimodal AI](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/kimi-k3-profile): Kimi K3 by Moonshot AI is a 2.8T open-weight model with a 1M-token context and native multimodal input. This is the reader's guide: what it is, what it takes to run, and whether the custom license fits your use.
- [Qwen3.8 Max: frontier AI you can run](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/qwen3-8-max-profile): Qwen3.8 Max is one of the strongest open-weight models of 2026. This is the owner's manual: what it is, what hardware it needs, what the license allows, and what it actually takes to run it yourself.
- [Running open models on school hardware](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/2026-running-open-weights-on-school-hardware): Most local AI advice assumes new GPUs. In a school with one lab of refurbished machines and an unreliable network, the real question is which small open-weight model a device can hold in memory and run at a classroom-friendly speed. Here is how to answer it.
- [Local AI privacy in 2026: the distributed option](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/2026-distributed-inference-privacy-reality): Self-hosted AI crossed into production use for many teams in 2026. But local is not automatically private, and distributed inference changes what a single site can run. Here is the honest check before you trust a deployment.
- [Edge and on-device AI, explained](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/2026-edge-on-device-ai-ai-pcs): About half of new PCs shipping in 2026 are projected to be AI PCs with dedicated neural processing units. Here is what the TOPS numbers mean, which small models run on them, and why on-device AI changes the privacy and offline story.
- [Hardware tiers for running local AI](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/2026-hardware-tiers-local-ai-inference): Local inference hardware has standardized into three tiers: edge devices for small models, workstations for mid-range models, and multi-GPU clusters for frontier architectures. Memory capacity and bandwidth, not raw FLOPS, set the binding constraint.
- [Quantization and MoE: model efficiency, explained](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/2026-quantization-moe-efficiency-memory-optimization): Quantization and Mixture-of-Experts routing are the two techniques that make large model inference feasible on consumer hardware. Here is how they work, what they cost in accuracy, and how to choose the right configuration.
- [Local AI runtimes: Ollama, vLLM & llama.cpp](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/2026-inference-runtimes-local-ai-tooling-maturity): Local inference runtimes have split into clear categories: desktop tools for prototyping, production servers for concurrent throughput, and core engines for edge hardware. Here is how to choose between them.
- [The 2026 open-weight model landscape](https://dintechnologies.com/blog/2026-open-weight-model-landscape-quality-gap): An evaluation of 2026 open-weight model families including DeepSeek V4, Qwen3.6, Llama 4, and Gemma 4, analyzing Mixture-of-Experts active parameter ratios, hardware VRAM floors, and commercial license constraints.
